title: Ἡ ἀρὰ τοῦ Κύκλωπος
about: Odysseus, still telling his story at the Phaeacian court, has got his ship away from the Cyclops’ island. Safely out at sea, he cannot resist taunting the blinded giant from the stern, and the Cyclops answers by tearing off the peak of a mountain and hurling it: it falls short, and the wave it raises carries the ship back toward the shore. Odysseus pushes off with a pole, and when the ship is twice as far out his companions beg him to say nothing more, since one more cry could bring a rock that smashes both ship and men. He will not be stopped, and shouts his real name and home to the Cyclops. The giant remembers an old prophecy by the seer Telemus, that he would lose his sight at the hands of Odysseus; he had expected a great and handsome man, not a small, feeble one who beat him with wine. He calls Odysseus back with offers of gifts and a safe conveyance from his father Poseidon. Odysseus answers that he wishes he could send him to the house of Hades, and the Cyclops prays to Poseidon: Odysseus must not reach home, but if it is his fate to do so, let him come late, in misery, having lost all his companions, on a strange ship, to trouble in his house. Poseidon hears; the Cyclops throws a much larger stone, which lands behind the ship, and its wave drives them to the island where the other ships and men are waiting. They share out the Cyclops’ flocks, Odysseus is given a ram as an extra and sacrifices it to Zeus, who takes no notice of the sacrifice and is already planning the loss of his ships and men. They feast, sleep, and at dawn put to sea, glad to have escaped death, though they have lost dear companions.

sentences.t:
Κύκλωψ, οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλες ἀνάλκιδος ἀνδρὸς ἑταίρους
ἔδμεναι ἐν σπῆι γλαφυρῷ κρατερῆφι βίηφι.
sentences.l:
‘Cyclops, not then were you going, of a man without might the companions
to eat in the hollow cave by strong force.
sentences.i: ‘Cyclops, so you were not, after all, going to eat the companions of a man without might in the hollow cave by strong force.
sentences.n: The speech is Odysseus's taunt from the ship, a speech inside his own telling; the previous part ends by announcing it. οὐκ ἄρ’ ἔμελλες is 'you were not, then, going to': ἔμελλες with an infinitive means 'were going to, were sure to', and ἄρ(α) marks a fact that has just turned out. ἀνάλκιδος is 'without might' (ἀ- 'not' + ἀλκή, the strength to defend oneself); the 'man without might' is Odysseus, as the Cyclops will say he took him to be at 513–516. ἔδμεναι is the epic infinitive of ἔδω 'eat', in -μεναι. σπῆι is the dative of σπέος 'cave'. κρατερῆφι βίηφι is 'by strong force': -φι is an old ending that does the work of 'by' or 'with'.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίην σέ γ’ ἔμελλε κιχήσεσθαι κακὰ ἔργα,
σχέτλι’, ἐπεὶ ξείνους οὐχ ἅζεο σῷ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
ἐσθέμεναι· τῷ σε Ζεὺς τίσατο καὶ θεοὶ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l:
And very much you it was bound to overtake, evil deeds,
Cruel one, since strangers you did not shrink-from, in your own house
to eat; therefore Zeus has punished you, and the other gods.’
sentences.i: Your evil deeds were bound to overtake you, Cruel one, since you did not shrink from eating strangers in your own house; therefore Zeus has punished you, and the other gods.’
sentences.n: The taunt turns on guest-right: the Cyclops ate guests, and Zeus, the god who looks after strangers, has paid him back. The subject comes late: κακὰ ἔργα 'evil deeds' is what was 'bound to overtake' (ἔμελλε κιχήσεσθαι, future infinitive of κιχάνω) the Cyclops, with σέ γε 'you, at least' as its object. καὶ λίην is 'and very much so, quite rightly'. σχέτλι’ is the vocative, the house 'Cruel one'. ξείνους is 'strangers'. ἅζεο is an imperfect of ἅζομαι 'shrink from, stand in awe of', followed by the infinitive ἐσθέμεναι 'to eat' (-μεναι again). τῷ is 'therefore'. τίσατο is the aorist middle of τίνυμαι, 'took vengeance on, punished'.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα χολώσατο κηρόθι μᾶλλον,
ἧκε δ’ ἀπορρήξας κορυφὴν ὄρεος μεγάλοιο,
κὰδ δ’ ἔβαλε προπάροιθε νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
τυτθόν, ἐδεύησεν δ’ οἰήιον ἄκρον ἱκέσθαι,
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and he then was angered more in his heart,
and hurled, having broken off, the peak of a great mountain,
and cast it down in front of the dark-prowed ship
a little way, and it fell short of reaching the tip of the steering-oar,
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he was angered the more at heart; he broke off the peak of a great mountain and hurled it, and cast it down a little way in front of the dark-prowed ship, and it fell short of reaching the tip of the steering-oar;
sentences.n: The taunt is over and Odysseus is narrating again: ὣς ἐφάμην is 'so I spoke', and ὁ 'he' is the Cyclops. χολώσατο is the aorist middle of χολόω 'make angry', used as 'was angered'; κηρόθι is 'in his heart' (κῆρ with the place-ending -θι), μᾶλλον 'more'. ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι 'hurled'; ὄρεος is Ionic for ὄρους, and μεγάλοιο is a genitive in -οιο. κὰδ … ἔβαλε is tmesis, κατέβαλε 'cast down', with κάδ as κατά before δ’. προπάροιθε takes the genitive: 'in front of'. τυτθόν 'a little', set off by a comma, goes with ἔβαλε. ἐδεύησεν … ἱκέσθαι is 'it lacked (something) to reach', that is 'fell short of reaching'; οἰήιον is the handle of the steering-oar, and ἄκρον 'the tip'.

sentences.t: ἐκλύσθη δὲ θάλασσα κατερχομένης ὑπὸ πέτρης·
sentences.l: and the sea was washed up in a surge beneath the descending rock;
sentences.i: and the sea surged up beneath the falling rock;
sentences.n: One line, a clause of its own. ἐκλύσθη is an aorist passive, 'was washed up, surged', from κλύζω 'wash, dash' (the ἐ- is the ordinary augment, not a preverb). κατερχομένης ὑπὸ πέτρης is a genitive with ὑπό, 'under the rock as it came down'; πέτρη is the same rock, the peak of 481, now a falling boulder. θάλασσα is 'the sea'.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ αἶψ’ ἤπειρόνδε παλιρρόθιον φέρε κῦμα,
πλημυρὶς ἐκ πόντοιο, θέμωσε δὲ χέρσον ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
and it quickly to the mainland the back-flowing wave bore,
a flood from the open-sea, and forced it to reach dry land.
sentences.i: and a wave, flowing back, quickly carried it toward the mainland, a flood from the open sea, and forced it to reach dry land.
sentences.n: τὴν 'it' is the ship (νεός, feminine νηῦς, in 482). ἤπειρόνδε is 'to the mainland': -δε marks the direction. παλιρρόθιον is 'back-flowing, rushing back' (πάλιν 'back' + ῥόθος 'rushing noise'), agreeing with κῦμα 'wave'. φέρε is 'carried', without augment. πλημυρίς 'flood, swell' stands in apposition to the wave; ἐκ πόντοιο is 'from the open-sea', πόντος being the house 'open-sea'. θέμωσε is a rare verb whose exact sense is not known; 'forced, drove' is what the context requires, and it returns at 542. χέρσον is 'dry land' as against the sea; it is distinct from ἤπειρος 'mainland'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ χείρεσσι λαβὼν περιμήκεα κοντὸν
ὦσα παρέξ, ἑτάροισι δ’ ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα
ἐμβαλέειν κώπῃς, ἵν’ ὑπὲκ κακότητα φύγοιμεν,
κρατὶ κατανεύων·
sentences.l:
But I, with my hands taking a very long pole,
pushed it off, and my companions, having urged on, I ordered
to throw themselves upon the oars, that out of harm we might flee,
by my head nodding;
sentences.i: But I took a very long pole in my hands and pushed the ship off, and urged my companions on and ordered them to throw themselves upon the oars, so that we might escape from our trouble, nodding with my head;
sentences.n: One long sentence of action. κοντόν is 'a pole', περιμήκεα 'very long'. ὦσα is the aorist of ὠθέω 'push'; παρέξ 'out of the way'; the ship is understood. ἑτάροισι δ’ ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα is 'having urged on, I ordered my companions': the participle and the verb are close to one act, and the dative ἑτάροισι, which ἐποτρύνω takes, serves for both. ἐμβαλέειν is the aorist infinitive 'to throw themselves in', and κώπῃς is a dative plural 'to the oars'. ὑπὲκ κακότητα is 'out from under harm'; κακότης is 'badness, trouble', and the preposition here takes the accusative. κρατὶ κατανεύων, 'nodding with the head', is a gesture that goes with the order.

sentences.t: οἱ δὲ προπεσόντες ἔρεσσον.
sentences.l: And they, falling forward, rowed.
sentences.i: They threw themselves forward and rowed.
sentences.n: A short sentence beginning in mid-line, after the ano teleia, and giving the crew's response. προπεσόντες is the aorist participle of προπίπτω 'fall forward', that is bend into the stroke; ἔρεσσον is the imperfect of ἐρέσσω 'row', and the imperfect gives the sense of a continuing effort. οἱ is 'they', the pronoun.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ δὶς τόσσον ἅλα πρήσσοντες ἀπῆμεν,
καὶ τότε δὴ Κύκλωπα προσηύδων·
sentences.l:
But when twice so much, the salt-sea making-our-way, we were away,
then indeed the Cyclops I spoke to;
sentences.i: But when we had gone twice as far over the salt sea, then I spoke to the Cyclops;
sentences.n: δὶς τόσσον is 'twice so much', that is twice the distance of the earlier taunt (9.473, in the last lines of the previous part). ἅλα πρήσσοντες is 'traversing the salt-sea' (ἅλα is the accusative of the ground covered): πρήσσω is the Ionic form of πράσσω, here 'accomplish, cover', and ἅλα is the house 'salt-sea'. ἀπῆμεν is the imperfect of ἄπειμι 'be away', 'we were at a distance'. προσηύδων is 'I spoke to' (the house word, as at 9.473); the imperfect is open about whether Odysseus gets to speak, and the next sentence shows that his companions hold him back. The ano teleia is rendered as a semicolon.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν ἐρήτυον ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος·
sentences.l:
but around, my companions
with gentle words were restraining me, one from one side, one from another:
sentences.i: but my companions all around me tried to hold me back with gentle words, one from one side and one from another:
sentences.n: The sentence begins in mid-line, after the ano teleia. ἀμφί here is an adverb, 'around'. μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσιν is 'with soothing words': μειλίχιος 'gentle' (the house word, as at 9.363) and ἔπος 'word', in a dative plural in -εσσι(ν). ἐρήτυον is the imperfect of ἐρητύω 'hold back, restrain'; its object, 'me', is not stated. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος is 'one from one place, another from another'. The colon promises the speech that follows.

sentences.t: σχέτλιε, τίπτ’ ἐθέλεις ἐρεθιζέμεν ἄγριον ἄνδρα;
sentences.l: ‘Cruel one, why do you wish to provoke a savage man?
sentences.i: ‘Cruel one, why do you want to provoke a savage man?
sentences.n: The companions' plea, with Odysseus as its target; Murray prints no quotation marks, and the English has them. σχέτλιε is the vocative of σχέτλιος, the house 'Cruel one', the same word as σχέτλι’ in 478. τίπτ’ is τί ποτε 'why ever'. ἐρεθιζέμεν is an infinitive in -έμεν, 'to provoke'. ἄγριον is the house 'savage'; the 'savage man' is the Cyclops.

sentences.t:
ὃς καὶ νῦν πόντονδε βαλὼν βέλος ἤγαγε νῆα
αὖτις ἐς ἤπειρον, καὶ δὴ φάμεν αὐτόθ’ ὀλέσθαι.
sentences.l:
who even now, into the open-sea having cast a missile, drove the ship
again to the mainland, and indeed we said we had perished on the spot.
sentences.i: Even now he threw a missile into the sea and drove the ship back to the mainland, and we thought we had perished on the spot.
sentences.n: The relative ὃς 'who' refers back to the Cyclops: the English begins a new sentence, 'he'. βέλος is 'a missile', here the mountain-peak. πόντονδε is 'into the open-sea': -δε marks direction, and πόντος is the house 'open-sea'. ἤγαγε is the aorist of ἄγω 'led, drove'; αὖτις 'back again'; ἐς ἤπειρον 'to the mainland'. φάμεν is the imperfect 'we said' (unaugmented), the infinitive ὀλέσθαι 'to have perished' (aorist middle of ὄλλυμι); 'we thought' is 'we said to ourselves'. αὐτόθ’ is αὐτόθι 'on the spot'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δὲ φθεγξαμένου τευ ἢ αὐδήσαντος ἄκουσε,
σύν κεν ἄραξ’ ἡμέων κεφαλὰς καὶ νήια δοῦρα
μαρμάρῳ ὀκριόεντι βαλών·
sentences.i: If he had heard anyone make a sound or speak, he would have smashed our heads and the ship’s timbers by throwing a jagged rock;
sentences.n: A condition contrary to fact: εἰ with the aorist ἄκουσε 'he had heard', and κεν with the aorist ἄραξε 'he would have smashed'. Verbs of hearing take the genitive of the sound or person heard, so φθεγξαμένου and αὐδήσαντος are genitive participles, 'one having uttered a sound or one having spoken', agreeing with τευ (= τινός, 'of anyone'). σύν … ἄραξ’ is tmesis, συνάραξε 'dashed together, smashed'. ἡμέων is the uncontracted genitive 'of us'. νήια δοῦρα is 'the ship’s timbers'. μαρμάρῳ is the dative of μάρμαρος 'a block of stone', here 'a rock'; ὀκριόεντι 'jagged', and βαλών 'having thrown'.

sentences.t: τόσσον γὰρ ἵησιν.
sentences.l: for so much he hurls.’
sentences.i: for so far does he hurl.’
sentences.n: The reason for the fear, and the end of the companions' speech. τόσσον is 'so much, so far', and the Greek does not say whether the force or the distance is meant; the English keeps 'so far', and the thought is the same. ἵησιν is the present of ἵημι 'send, hurl'; γάρ 'for'.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάσαν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πεῖθον ἐμὸν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν,
ἀλλά μιν ἄψορρον προσέφην κεκοτηότι θυμῷ·
sentences.l:
So they spoke, but they were not persuading my great-spirited heart,
but I addressed him, back again, with an angered heart:
sentences.i: So they spoke, but they did not persuade my great-spirited heart; and I addressed him again, with an angry heart:
sentences.n: A narrative couplet between two speeches, with no speaker to mark. φάσαν is 'they spoke', the plural of the house 'So he spoke' formula. πεῖθον is the imperfect of πείθω 'persuade', 'they were not persuading'. μεγαλήτορα is the house 'great-spirited', and θυμόν the 'heart'. μιν is 'him', the Cyclops. ἄψορρον is 'back' or 'backward'; the exact force of this adverb with προσέφην is not certain, and 'again' is a plain reading. προσέφην is 'I addressed', a past tense of πρόσφημι. κεκοτηότι is a perfect participle of κοτέω 'bear a grudge, be angry', in the dative: 'with an angered heart'.

sentences.t:
Κύκλωψ, αἴ κέν τίς σε καταθνητῶν ἀνθρώπων
ὀφθαλμοῦ εἴρηται ἀεικελίην ἀλαωτύν,
φάσθαι Ὀδυσσῆα πτολιπόρθιον ἐξαλαῶσαι,
υἱὸν Λαέρτεω, Ἰθάκῃ ἔνι οἰκί’ ἔχοντα.
sentences.l:
‘Cyclops, if any of mortal men you
asks about the unseemly blinding of the eye,
say that Odysseus the city-sacking blinded you,
the son of Laertes, who has his dwellings in Ithaca.’
sentences.i: ‘Cyclops, if any of mortal men asks you about the shameful blinding of your eye, say that Odysseus, sacker of cities, blinded you, the son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca.’
sentences.n: Odysseus now gives his true name, not the 'Nobody' of the previous part, and against his companions' advice. αἴ κέν is 'if ever': αἲ is a form of εἰ, used before κε. εἴρηται is a subjunctive of εἴρομαι 'ask', with two accusatives, 'asks you the blinding'; ὀφθαλμοῦ is 'of the eye'. ἀεικελίην is 'unseemly', here 'shameful', and ἀλαωτύν 'blinding'. φάσθαι is the infinitive of φημί used as an imperative, 'say!'. ἐξαλαῶσαι is the aorist infinitive 'blinded'. πτολιπόρθιον is the epithet of Odysseus, 'city-sacking' (πτολί- is the old form of πολι- 'city'; πέρθω 'sack'), and Λαέρτεω is a genitive in -εω (= -ου). οἰκί’ is the plural 'dwellings'.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ οἰμώξας ἠμείβετο μύθῳ·
sentences.l: So I spoke, and he, groaning, answered me with a word:
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he groaned and answered me:
sentences.n: A reply-formula, new in this form: ὣς ἐφάμην is 'so I spoke', and in ὁ δέ μ’ οἰμώξας ἠμείβετο μύθῳ the ὁ is 'he'; οἰμώξας is the aorist participle of οἰμώζω 'groan, wail'; ἠμείβετο the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι 'answer'; μύθῳ 'with a word, a speech'.

sentences.t: ὢ πόποι, ἦ μάλα δή με παλαίφατα θέσφαθ’ ἱκάνει.
sentences.l: ‘Ah, truly indeed now me the long-ago-spoken god-declared things are reaching.
sentences.i: ‘Ah, the prophecies spoken long ago are truly coming upon me now.
sentences.n: The Cyclops' own speech starts: he remembers a prophecy. ὢ πόποι is 'Ah'. ἦ μάλα δή is 'truly indeed'. παλαίφατα is 'spoken long ago' (παλαι- 'long ago' + φατός 'spoken'), agreeing with θέσφαθ’, a neuter plural from θέσφατος 'declared by a god', that is oracle or prophecy. As a neuter plural subject it takes a singular verb, ἱκάνει, from ἱκάνω 'come to, reach', with με as object.

sentences.t:
ἔσκε τις ἐνθάδε μάντις ἀνὴρ ἠύς τε μέγας τε,
Τήλεμος Εὐρυμίδης, ὃς μαντοσύνῃ ἐκέκαστο
καὶ μαντευόμενος κατεγήρα Κυκλώπεσσιν·
sentences.i: There was a seer here, a good and great man, Telemus, son of Eurymus, who excelled in the art of prophecy and grew old prophesying among the Cyclopes;
sentences.n: The seer Telemus is introduced with his father's name. ἔσκε is the imperfect of εἰμί with the suffix -σκ-: 'there was'. ἠύς is 'good, brave'. Εὐρυμίδης is a patronymic, 'son of Eurymus'. μαντοσύνῃ is a dative, 'in seercraft' (μάντις 'seer'), and ἐκέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι (κέκασμαι), 'had excelled' with a past sense. κατεγήρα is the imperfect of καταγηράω 'grow old', and Κυκλώπεσσιν is a dative plural in -εσσι: 'among the Cyclopes'.

sentences.t:
ὅς μοι ἔφη τάδε πάντα τελευτήσεσθαι ὀπίσσω,
χειρῶν ἐξ Ὀδυσῆος ἁμαρτήσεσθαι ὀπωπῆς.
sentences.l:
who told me that all these things would be fulfilled hereafter,
that I would lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus.
sentences.i: He told me that all this would be fulfilled in time to come, and that I should lose my sight at the hands of Odysseus.
sentences.n: The prophecy itself, in two lines. ὅς is the relative, 'who'. ἔφη is 'he said' (φημί). τελευτήσεσθαι is the future infinitive of τελευτάω 'fulfil, bring to pass', in the passive sense 'would be fulfilled', and ὀπίσσω is 'hereafter'. ἁμαρτήσεσθαι is the future infinitive of ἁμαρτάνω 'miss, lose', which takes the genitive ὀπωπῆς 'sight'. χειρῶν ἐξ Ὀδυσῆος is 'from the hands of Odysseus'. Murray prints Ὀδυσῆος here, Ὀδυσσῆα in 504 and Ὀδυσεῦ in 517: the name has the double σ or not as the metre requires.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ αἰεί τινα φῶτα μέγαν καὶ καλὸν ἐδέγμην
ἐνθάδ’ ἐλεύσεσθαι, μεγάλην ἐπιειμένον ἀλκήν·
sentences.l:
But always some man, big and fine, I was expecting
to come here, clothed in great might;
sentences.i: But I always expected some big, fine man to come here, clothed in great might;
sentences.n: The Cyclops' expectation. φῶτα is the accusative of φώς 'man'. μέγαν καὶ καλόν is 'big and fine'. ἐδέγμην is a past form of δέχομαι 'await, expect'. ἐλεύσεσθαι is the future infinitive 'to come'. ἐπιειμένον is the perfect participle of ἐπιέννυμι 'clothe', 'clothed in great might', with ἀλκήν 'might', the strength to fight; the same word is in ἀνάλκιδος 'without might' at 475.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ μ’ ἐὼν ὀλίγος τε καὶ οὐτιδανὸς καὶ ἄκικυς
ὀφθαλμοῦ ἀλάωσεν, ἐπεί μ’ ἐδαμάσσατο οἴνῳ.
sentences.l:
but now me, he being small and worthless and feeble,
of the eye he blinded, since he overpowered me with wine;
sentences.i: but now one who is small, worthless and feeble has blinded me in the eye, since he overpowered me with wine;
sentences.n: νῦν δέ sets the reality against the expectation. ἐών is the participle 'being', agreeing with the unstated subject 'he', Odysseus. ὀλίγος is 'small'. οὐτιδανός is the house 'worthless'. ἄκικυς is 'feeble' only from context: its derivation is not known. ὀφθαλμοῦ is a genitive of the thing taken away (ἀλάωσεν, 'blinded'), so 'blinded me of the eye', that is 'blinded my eye'. ἐδαμάσσατο is the aorist middle of δαμάζω 'overpower'; οἴνῳ is a dative 'with wine'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δεῦρ’, Ὀδυσεῦ, ἵνα τοι πὰρ ξείνια θείω
πομπήν τ’ ὀτρύνω δόμεναι κλυτὸν ἐννοσίγαιον·
sentences.l:
But come here, Odysseus, so that for you I may set out gifts of hospitality
and urge the famous earth-shaker to give you an escort;
sentences.i: But come here, Odysseus, so that I may set out for you the gifts due a guest and urge the famous earth-shaker to give you an escort;
sentences.n: The Cyclops now tries to call Odysseus back with an offer. ἀλλ’ ἄγε is 'but come'. ἵνα … θείω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive; πὰρ is παρά 'beside', in tmesis with θείω: 'set beside, set out'. ξείνια are 'gifts of hospitality', the things due to a guest. πομπήν is the house 'escort'; ὀτρύνω is the subjunctive 'I may urge'; δόμεναι is the infinitive in -μεναι, 'to give'. κλυτὸν ἐννοσίγαιον is the house 'the famous earth-shaker', Poseidon.

sentences.t: τοῦ γὰρ ἐγὼ πάϊς εἰμί, πατὴρ δ’ ἐμὸς εὔχεται εἶναι.
sentences.l: for of him I am the son, and my father he claims to be.
sentences.i: for I am his son, and he claims to be my father.
sentences.n: τοῦ is 'of him', and the genitive of 'him' belongs to πάϊς, the epic form of παῖς 'child, son'. The Cyclops is Poseidon's son, and the father 'claims' it: εὔχεται means 'claims, boasts' here, as it means 'prays' at 527. It is the same verb, and the sense depends on the context.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’, αἴ κ’ ἐθέλῃσ’, ἰήσεται, οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
οὔτε θεῶν μακάρων οὔτε θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων.
sentences.l:
And he himself, if he wishes, will heal, and no one else,
neither of the blessed gods nor of mortal men.’
sentences.i: He himself will heal it, if he wishes, and no one else will, whether of the blessed gods or of mortal men.’
sentences.n: The Cyclops' conclusion: only Poseidon can heal his eye. αὐτός is 'he himself'. αἴ κ’ is 'if ever' (αἲ … κε). ἰήσεται is the future middle of ἰάομαι 'heal'; its object, the eye, is understood. οὐδέ τις ἄλλος … οὔτε … οὔτε is 'and no one else, neither … nor', with the genitives θεῶν μακάρων 'of the blessed gods' and θνητῶν ἀνθρώπων 'of mortal men'.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: An already published line, so its English is exactly the earlier English. ὣς ἔφατ’ is 'so he/she spoke' (ἔφατο with its last vowel dropped), and the Greek verb does not say which. The published English has 'she' and 'her', from an earlier part where a woman spoke; here the speaker is the Cyclops, so read 'she' and 'her' as 'he' and 'him'. αὐτάρ is 'but, and'; ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is 'answering I addressed'.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ δὴ ψυχῆς τε καὶ αἰῶνός σε δυναίμην
εὖνιν ποιήσας πέμψαι δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω,
ὡς οὐκ ὀφθαλμόν γ’ ἰήσεται οὐδ’ ἐνοσίχθων.
sentences.l:
‘Would that, of life and of lifetime you, I could
bereft make and send to the house of Hades within,
so surely as not the eye even the earth-shaker will heal.’
sentences.i: ‘If only I could rob you of your life and your lifetime and send you down into the house of Hades, as surely as not even the earth-shaker will heal your eye.’
sentences.n: Odysseus's answer is a wish. αἲ γάρ … δυναίμην is a wish with the optative: 'would that I could'. εὖνιν is 'bereft', agreeing with σέ, and the genitives ψυχῆς and αἰῶνος 'of life, of lifetime' show what is lost. δυναίμην governs the aorist infinitive πέμψαι 'to send', and ποιήσας 'having made' goes with εὖνιν: 'having made you bereft'. δόμον Ἄϊδος εἴσω is 'into the house of Hades'. ὡς here means 'as surely as': ὡς οὐκ … ἰήσεται is 'as certainly as … will not heal'. ἐνοσίχθων is the house 'earth-shaker', the god the Cyclops has just named as the only healer.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δ’ ἔπειτα Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι
εὔχετο χεῖρ’ ὀρέγων εἰς οὐρανὸν ἀστερόεντα·
sentences.l:
So I spoke, and he then to Poseidon the lord
prayed, stretching out his hands to the starry sky:
sentences.i: So I spoke, and he then prayed to lord Poseidon, stretching out his hands to the starry sky:
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is 'so I spoke'. Ποσειδάωνι ἄνακτι is 'to Poseidon the lord', dative; εὔχετο is the imperfect of εὔχομαι, here 'prayed', as it was 'claims' in 519. χεῖρ’ is χεῖρε or χεῖρα, the dual or the singular with the last vowel dropped; 'hands' is the plain English for a prayer. ὀρέγων is 'stretching out', and ἀστερόεντα is 'starry', agreeing with οὐρανόν 'the sky'. The colon promises the prayer.

sentences.t:
κλῦθι, Ποσείδαον γαιήοχε κυανοχαῖτα,
εἰ ἐτεόν γε σός εἰμι, πατὴρ δ’ ἐμὸς εὔχεαι εἶναι,
δὸς μὴ Ὀδυσσῆα πτολιπόρθιον οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι
υἱὸν Λαέρτεω, Ἰθάκῃ ἔνι οἰκί’ ἔχοντα.
sentences.l:
‘Hear, Poseidon earth-holder, dark-haired one,
if truly I am yours, and my father you claim to be,
grant that Odysseus the city-sacking not reach home,
the son of Laertes, who has his dwellings in Ithaca.
sentences.i: ‘Hear me, Poseidon, earth-holder, dark-haired one; if I am truly yours, and you claim to be my father, grant that Odysseus, sacker of cities, not reach home, the son of Laertes, who has his home in Ithaca.
sentences.n: The prayer, which is a curse. κλῦθι is 'hear', imperative of κλύω. γαιήοχε is the house 'earth-holder', and κυανοχαῖτα the vocative of κυανοχαίτης 'dark-haired': the house 'dark-haired earth-shaker' has the same epithet. εἰ ἐτεόν γε σός εἰμι is 'if indeed I am yours' (ἐτεόν 'truly'), with εὔχεαι 'you claim', in the form -εαι that Attic contracts to -ῃ. δὸς μὴ … ἱκέσθαι is 'grant that he not reach', with the aorist infinitive. Line 531 is word for word line 505, Odysseus's own description of himself, now in his enemy's mouth, and its English is the same. πτολιπόρθιον is the house 'city-sacking'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ οἱ μοῖρ’ ἐστὶ φίλους τ’ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι
οἶκον ἐυκτίμενον καὶ ἑὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν,
ὀψὲ κακῶς ἔλθοι, ὀλέσας ἄπο πάντας ἑταίρους,
νηὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίης, εὕροι δ’ ἐν πήματα οἴκῳ.
sentences.l:
But if for him it is fate to see his dear ones and to reach
his well-built house and his own fatherland,
late and badly may he come, having lost all his companions,
on another’s ship, and may he find troubles in his house.’
sentences.i: But if it is his fate to see his dear ones and to reach his well-built house and his own fatherland, then let him come late and in misery, having lost all his companions, on a ship not his own, and let him find troubles in his house.’
sentences.n: The second half of the curse, a qualification. εἴ οἱ μοῖρ’ ἐστί is 'if it is fate for him', with the infinitives ἰδέειν 'to see' and ἱκέσθαι 'to reach'. φίλους are 'dear ones'. ἐυκτίμενον is 'well-built'. ἑήν is the possessive 'his own'; πατρίδα … γαῖαν is 'fatherland'. ἔλθοι and εὕροι are optatives of wish: 'may he come', 'may he find'. ὀλέσας ἄπο is tmesis, ἀπολέσας 'having lost'. νηὸς ἐπ’ ἀλλοτρίης is 'on a ship of another' (ἀλλότριος 'belonging to another'). ἐν … οἴκῳ is 'in his house', the preposition set apart from its noun. The end of the Cyclops' speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε κυανοχαίτης.
sentences.l: So he spoke, praying, and him heard the dark-haired one.
sentences.i: So he prayed, and the dark-haired god heard him.
sentences.n: The prayer is answered at once. ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος is the house 'So he spoke, praying'. τοῦ is a genitive, as verbs of hearing take, 'him', and ἔκλυε is the aorist of κλύω 'hear'. κυανοχαίτης stands alone for Poseidon: 'the dark-haired one'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ ἐξαῦτις πολὺ μείζονα λᾶαν ἀείρας
ἧκ’ ἐπιδινήσας, ἐπέρεισε δὲ ἶν’ ἀπέλεθρον,
κὰδ’ δ’ ἔβαλεν μετόπισθε νεὸς κυανοπρῴροιο
τυτθόν, ἐδεύησεν δ’ οἰήιον ἄκρον ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l:
But he again a much greater stone lifting
hurled it, having swung it round, and pressed upon it measureless strength,
and cast it down behind the dark-prowed ship
a little way, and it fell short of reaching the tip of the steering-oar;
sentences.i: But he again lifted a much greater stone and, swinging it round, hurled it, and put measureless strength behind it, and cast it down a little way behind the dark-prowed ship, and it fell short of reaching the tip of the steering-oar;
sentences.n: The second throw, set against the first, 482–483. ἐξαῦτις is 'again'; πολὺ μείζονα is 'much greater', and λᾶαν the accusative of λᾶας 'stone'. ἀείρας is 'having lifted', ἧκ’ 'he hurled', ἐπιδινήσας 'having swung it round'. ἐπέρεισε δὲ ἶν’ ἀπέλεθρον is 'and pressed measureless strength upon it': ἶν’ is the accusative of ἴς 'strength'; ἀπέλεθρον may come from πέλεθρον, a measure of length, but the formation is not certain. Murray prints κὰδ’ δ’ at the start of 539; κατά loses its last syllable by apocope, which needs no apostrophe, so read the κὰδ δ’ of 482. μετόπισθε is 'behind', where 482 had προπάροιθε 'in front of'; 540 repeats 483 with a full stop for its comma.

sentences.t: ἐκλύσθη δὲ θάλασσα κατερχομένης ὑπὸ πέτρης·
sentences.l: and the sea was washed up in a surge beneath the descending rock;
sentences.i: and the sea surged up beneath the falling rock;
sentences.n: The same line as 484, in the same words, now for the second throw; the English is the same as there, and the notes on ἐκλύσθη and κατερχομένης ὑπὸ πέτρης are at that line.

sentences.t: τὴν δὲ πρόσω φέρε κῦμα, θέμωσε δὲ χέρσον ἱκέσθαι.
sentences.l: and it forward the wave bore, and forced it to reach dry land.
sentences.i: and the wave carried it forward, and forced it to reach dry land.
sentences.n: A shorter form of 485–486: τὴν is the ship, πρόσω 'forward', and φέρε κῦμα 'the wave carried'. θέμωσε is the same rare verb as at 486, and its sense is no better known here (see the note there); 'forced' is what the context requires. χέρσον is 'dry land'; here it is the island reached in the next lines.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τὴν νῆσον ἀφικόμεθ’, ἔνθα περ ἄλλαι
νῆες ἐύσσελμοι μένον ἁθρόαι, ἀμφὶ δ’ ἑταῖροι
ἥατ’ ὀδυρόμενοι, ἡμέας ποτιδέγμενοι αἰεί,
sentences.l:
But when we reached the island, just where the other
well-benched ships were waiting, all together, and around, the companions
sat lamenting, for us always waiting,
sentences.i: But when we reached the island, just where the other well-benched ships were waiting all together, and the companions sat around them lamenting, always waiting for us,
sentences.n: A long subordinate clause, with its main verbs in the next unit. τὴν νῆσον is 'the island', with the article nearly 'that'. ἔνθα περ is 'just where'. ἐύσσελμοι is the house 'well-benched', of the ships, and ἁθρόαι 'all together, in a body'. ἀμφί is an adverb, 'around'. ἥατ’ is ἥατο, the epic imperfect plural of ἧμαι 'sit' (-ατο for -ντο), with ὀδυρόμενοι 'lamenting'. ποτιδέγμενοι is 'waiting for', from προσδέχομαι with ποτί for πρός, and ἡμέας is 'us'. αἰεί 'always'.

sentences.t:
νῆα μὲν ἔνθ’ ἐλθόντες ἐκέλσαμεν ἐν ψαμάθοισιν,
ἐκ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ βῆμεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
the ship, there having come, we ran ashore in the sands,
and out too we ourselves stepped upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: Coming there, we ran the ship ashore on the sands, and we ourselves too stepped out onto the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: The main verbs of the sentence. νῆα μὲν … ἐκ δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ is 'the ship … and we ourselves': μέν and δέ set the ship against the men. ἐκέλσαμεν is the aorist of κέλλω 'run a ship ashore'. ψαμάθοισιν is a dative plural of ψάμαθος 'sand'. βῆμεν is the unaugmented aorist 'we stepped', with ἐκ 'out'. ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης is the house 'upon the surf-line of the sea', that is the shore where the sea breaks. The second line is the same as one published earlier, and its English is kept.

sentences.t:
μῆλα δὲ Κύκλωπος γλαφυρῆς ἐκ νηὸς ἑλόντες
δασσάμεθ’, ὡς μή τίς μοι ἀτεμβόμενος κίοι ἴσης.
sentences.l:
And the flocks of the Cyclops, out of the hollow ship taking,
we shared out, so that no man, for me, cheated, should go off short of an equal share.
sentences.i: And taking the Cyclops’ flocks out of the hollow ship, we shared them out, so that no man, on my account, should go away cheated of an equal share.
sentences.n: μῆλα are 'flocks', the small livestock, sheep and goats together. γλαφυρῆς is the house 'hollow', of the ship. ἑλόντες is 'having taken', and δασσάμεθ’ is the aorist middle of δατέομαι 'divide, share out'. The second line is one published earlier, and its English is kept: ὡς μή is 'so that … not', ἀτεμβόμενος is 'cheated', and κίοι is the optative of κίω 'go'. ἴσης is a genitive of what is lacking: 'short of an equal share'.

sentences.t:
ἀρνειὸν δ’ ἐμοὶ οἴῳ ἐυκνήμιδες ἑταῖροι
μήλων δαιομένων δόσαν ἔξοχα· τὸν δ’ ἐπὶ θινὶ
Ζηνὶ κελαινεφέι Κρονίδῃ, ὃς πᾶσιν ἀνάσσει,
ῥέξας μηρί’ ἔκαιον·
sentences.l:
And a ram, to me alone, my well-greaved companions
gave, from the flocks being divided, as an extra; and him, on the beach,
to Zeus dark-clouded, son of Cronus, who rules over all,
having sacrificed, I burned thigh-pieces;
sentences.i: And my well-greaved companions gave me alone a ram, as an extra, when the flocks were being divided; and on the beach I sacrificed it to Zeus of the dark clouds, son of Cronus, who rules over all, and burned the thigh-pieces;
sentences.n: The ram is the extra share for Odysseus, which he gives to Zeus. ἀρνειόν is 'ram'; ἐυκνήμιδες is the house 'well-greaved', of companions as of Achaeans. μήλων δαιομένων is 'the flocks being divided': the genitive can be read as 'out of the flocks' (l) or as 'while they were being divided' (i), and the Greek does not choose. δόσαν is the unaugmented 'they gave', and ἔξοχα 'outstandingly', here 'as an extra'. τὸν is 'it', the ram, and ἐπὶ θινί 'on the beach'. κελαινεφέι is 'of the dark clouds' (κελαινός 'dark' + νέφος 'cloud'), set against the house 'cloud-gatherer'. ῥέξας is the aorist of ῥέζω, used of sacrifice, and μηρία 'thigh-pieces' are the parts burned for the gods.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ οὐκ ἐμπάζετο ἱρῶν,
ἀλλ’ ὅ γε μερμήριξεν ὅπως ἀπολοίατο πᾶσαι
νῆες ἐύσσελμοι καὶ ἐμοὶ ἐρίηρες ἑταῖροι.
sentences.l:
and he took no heed of the sacrifices,
but he pondered how there might perish, all
the well-benched ships and my trusty companions.
sentences.i: but he took no heed of the sacrifices, and pondered how all the well-benched ships and my trusty companions might perish.
sentences.n: The sentence begins in mid-line after the ano teleia. ὁ is 'he', and the god in question is Zeus, from the previous unit, not the Cyclops. ἐμπάζετο is 'took heed of' and takes the genitive ἱρῶν 'of the sacrifices'. μερμήριξεν is the aorist of μερμηρίζω 'ponder'. ὅπως ἀπολοίατο is 'how they might perish', an optative ending in -οίατο. πᾶσαι νῆες ἐύσσελμοι is 'all the well-benched ships'. ἐρίηρες is the house 'trusty'; the exact sense of ἐρίηρος is not fully known.

sentences.t:
ὣς τότε μὲν πρόπαν ἦμαρ ἐς ἠέλιον καταδύντα
ἥμεθα δαινύμενοι κρέα τ’ ἄσπετα καὶ μέθυ ἡδύ·
sentences.l:
So then for the whole day, until the sun going down,
we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.i: So for that whole day, until the sun went down, we sat feasting on boundless meat and sweet wine;
sentences.n: A published pair of lines, with its English kept. ἥμεθα is the imperfect of ἧμαι 'sit', 'we sat'; δαινύμενοι 'feasting'. ἄσπετα is 'boundless'. The ano teleia is rendered as a semicolon. πρόπαν ἦμαρ is 'the whole day'.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠέλιος κατέδυ καὶ ἐπὶ κνέφας ἦλθε,
δὴ τότε κοιμήθημεν ἐπὶ ῥηγμῖνι θαλάσσης.
sentences.l:
And when the sun set and darkness came on,
then indeed we lay down to sleep upon the surf-line of the sea.
sentences.i: And when the sun set and darkness came on, then we lay down to sleep on the shore where the sea breaks.
sentences.n: Another published pair. ἦμος is 'when' and ἠέλιος κατέδυ 'the sun set'. κνέφας is 'darkness'. δὴ τότε is 'then indeed', and κοιμήθημεν 'we lay down to sleep', the aorist passive of κοιμάω.

sentences.t:
ἦμος δ’ ἠριγένεια φάνη ῥοδοδάκτυλος Ἠώς,
δὴ τότ’ ἐγὼν ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα
αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι·
sentences.i: When early-born Dawn appeared, rose-fingered, then I urged my companions on and ordered them to embark themselves and to cast off the stern-cables;
sentences.n: The first line is the house 'When early-born appeared, rose-fingered Dawn'. ἐγών is ἐγώ in epic. ἑτάροισιν ἐποτρύνας ἐκέλευσα is 'having urged on my companions, I ordered', as at 488. αὐτούς τ’ ἀμβαίνειν ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι is 'themselves to embark and to loose the stern-cables'; ἀνὰ … λῦσαι is tmesis, ἀναλῦσαι 'loose', and the infinitive ἀμβαίνειν is for ἀναβαίνειν (ἀν- assimilated before β). The first and third lines are as published before, and their English is kept.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ αἶψ’ εἴσβαινον καὶ ἐπὶ κληῖσι καθῖζον,
ἑξῆς δ’ ἑζόμενοι πολιὴν ἅλα τύπτον ἐρετμοῖς.
sentences.l:
And they quickly went aboard and on the rowing-benches sat down,
and sitting in a row, the grey sea they struck with their oars.
sentences.i: They quickly went aboard and sat down at the oarlocks, and sitting in rows, they struck the grey sea with their oars.
sentences.n: A published pair. εἴσβαινον 'they went aboard' and καθῖζον 'they sat down' are unaugmented imperfects; ἐπὶ κληῖσι is the house 'at the oarlocks'. ἑξῆς is 'in order'. πολιὴν ἅλα is the house 'the grey sea', and ἐρετμοῖς 'with oars'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δὲ προτέρω πλέομεν ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ,
ἄσμενοι ἐκ θανάτοιο, φίλους ὀλέσαντες ἑταίρους.
sentences.l:
From there farther we sailed, grieved in heart,
glad to be out of death, dear companions having lost.
sentences.i: From there we sailed on, grieved at heart, glad to be out of death, though we had lost our dear companions.
sentences.n: A published pair. ἔνθεν is 'from there', προτέρω 'farther', πλέομεν 'we sailed'. ἀκαχήμενοι ἦτορ is the house 'grieved at heart', and ἄσμενοι ἐκ θανάτοιο 'glad to be out of death'. The last words, φίλους ὀλέσαντες ἑταίρους, say what the escape cost. The end of Odysseus's account of this episode.
